summary: An informational memo defining the initial assignment of IPv6 multicast addresses.

plainLanguage.summary: A list of which special group addresses on the newer internet are reserved for what.

questions: how are ipv6 multicast addresses allocated
what multicast address is used for ospf
subtitle: The registry of reserved IPv6 multicast group addresses and their purposes.

tldr.problem: IPv6 multicast allows one sender to deliver a single packet to many receivers at once by addressing a group address rather than individual addresses. The internet needs a shared registry to ensure that two different services don't claim the same group address and cause collisions.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2375 defines the initial allocations of the multicast address space: link-local groups for essential protocols (OSPF routers, DHCPv6 agents), site-local groups, and globally scoped groups for services like NTP and multimedia conferences. The allocation follows IPv6 addressing rules and maps IPv4 multicast conventions to IPv6 equivalents.
tldr.outcome: The registry established a foundation for interoperable IPv6 multicast deployments. Devices and protocols can rely on well-known group addresses without coordinating out-of-band.

today: RFC 2375 is an Informational document that established the foundation for IPv6 multicast address allocation. IANA maintains the current registry and continues to assign addresses for new protocols according to the procedures outlined here and in the IPv6 Addressing Architecture.

sections.title: Multicast Addresses in IPv6
sections.content:
Multicast in IP networks allows a sender to transmit one packet to many receivers simultaneously. Instead of sending separate unicast packets to each recipient, a sender addresses a single multicast group address. Routers forward that packet to all networks with at least one listener on that group. Receivers signal their interest using a group membership protocol (IGMP for IPv4, MLD for IPv6).

Multicast is useful for broadcast-like services: all routers on a link need to hear OSPF routing updates, all DHCP clients need to discover DHCP servers, all nodes in a multimedia conference need each other's video streams. Without multicast, the sender would have to send individual copies to each recipient, wasting bandwidth.

IPv6 multicast addresses are allocated from a reserved portion of the address space. The first octet (FF in hex) identifies an address as multicast. Within the multicast space, addresses are allocated hierarchically: some are permanently reserved for specific protocols, others are allocated dynamically to applications, and some ranges are left unassigned for future use.
sections.plainLanguage: Multicast is like shouting in a stadium so everyone interested hears you at once, instead of calling each person individually. IPv6 sets aside special addresses that mean "all routers" or "all DHCP servers" so devices can find them without asking.

sections.title: Scope Boundaries and Allocation Strategy
sections.content:
IPv6 multicast addresses include a scope field that limits how far the packet travels. Node-local scope means the packet does not leave the sending computer. Link-local scope means the packet reaches only the local Ethernet segment (or wireless LAN); routers do not forward it further. Site-local scope reaches all computers within a site (organization), but not beyond to the internet. Global scope allows packets to be routed across the entire internet.

The allocation strategy preserves interoperability. Link-local addresses (FF02::/16) are reserved for protocols that must work automatically without manual configuration: all nodes on a link need to receive Router Advertisements, DHCP server discovery, and OSPF updates. Well-known addresses like FF02::1 (all nodes) and FF02::2 (all routers) are fixed. Specific link-local groups are assigned to protocols: FF02::5 for OSPF routers, FF02::9 for RIP routers, FF02::D for PIM routers.

Global multicast addresses (FF0X::/16 with variable scope) allow applications to operate across the internet. Some are permanently assigned to services like NTP (FF0X::101) and multimedia conferences (FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:2:0000 through FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:2:7FFF). Others are left unassigned for dynamic allocation or experimental use.
sections.plainLanguage: Some multicast addresses only work on your local network (link-local), some work within your organization (site-local), and some work globally across the internet. The registry reserves certain addresses for each protocol so they don't collide.

sections.title: The Address Registry
sections.content:
The RFC documents the initial assignments across multiple scope levels. Link-local scope (FF02::/16) allocates addresses for automatic protocols. FF02::1 and FF02::2 are all-nodes and all-routers addresses required by IPv6. Routing protocols each get a reserved address: OSPFIGP uses FF02::5 and FF02::6, RIPng uses FF02::9, EIGRP uses FF02::A. Service discovery protocols like Service Location (SLP) are assigned to FF05::116 (site-local).

Global multicast addresses include assignments to well-known services. NTP (Network Time Protocol) uses FF0X::101. Multimedia conference calls use a large range (FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:2:0000 through FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:2:7FFF). Session Announcement Protocol (SAP) announcements use FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:2:7FFE and FF0X:0:0:0:0:0:2:7FFF.

The document notes that IPv4 multicast conventions have been adapted where relevant; IPv4 assignments that do not apply to IPv6 (such as some legacy protocols) are omitted. The registry is structured to allow for future expansion: undefined ranges are reserved rather than assigned, permitting IANA to allocate them for new services without revising this document.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry is a phone book. FF02::5 is OSPF routers' number. FF02::101 is NTP's number. When a router boots, it sends to FF02::2 and says "I'm here, give me a routing update". No coordination needed because everyone uses the same numbers.

sections.title: Compatibility and Future Allocation
sections.content:
The RFC is based on the IPv6 Addressing Architecture (RFC 2373) and adapted from IPv4 multicast address assignments in the IANA registry. The goal is to ensure that IPv6 multicast implementations can be compatible with existing IPv4 deployments where the protocols are the same. For example, both IPv4 and IPv6 OSPF use their respective multicast addresses, so a dual-stack router (supporting both IPv4 and IPv6) can participate in multicast on each address family.

One key principle: addresses that differ only in scope represent different groups. FF01::1 (all nodes, node-local scope) is a different multicast group from FF02::1 (all nodes, link-local scope), even though both carry the same logical meaning. A node that wants to join both must join each address separately.

The RFC does not prescribe the mechanism for allocating unassigned ranges; it defers to IANA procedures and to the IPv6 Addressing Architecture for rules on how new addresses should be assigned. This forward-looking approach allows the registry to grow as IPv6 and new multicast applications evolve.
sections.plainLanguage: The registry is designed so IPv6 multicast works like IPv4 multicast where they overlap. Both support OSPF routers at their respective multicast addresses. When new services need addresses, IANA can assign them without breaking this document.
